title: Continuation of the National Emergency With Respect to Significant Narcotics Traffickers Centered in Colombia
summary:
The White House has extended for another year the national emergency focused on major drug traffickers centered in Colombia, a policy first put in place in 1995. The administration says these networks still pose an unusual and extraordinary threat to the United States, fueling violence, corruption, and economic harm at home and abroad.

This extension keeps in place tools that let the government identify, block, and penalize traffickers and their support networks. It benefits law enforcement and financial watchdogs by preserving authorities they use to go after illicit money and disrupt criminal organizations. Communities affected by drug-related crime may see continued pressure on the networks that fuel it. Businesses and banks also gain clarity that existing restrictions and screening practices remain in force, which can help protect them from unknowingly handling risky transactions. Colombian authorities and international partners may find continued support for joint efforts against organized crime.

On the other hand, people or companies tied to these networks can face frozen assets and limits on doing business in the United States. There is also a risk that legitimate firms, especially those operating in or with Colombia, could encounter higher compliance costs, delayed transactions, or banks pulling back from certain relationships out of caution. If mistakes occur in identifying targets, affected parties may need to navigate a difficult process to correct the record. The policy can also add strain to diplomatic and commercial ties if its impact is felt beyond the intended targets.

The notice will be published and sent to Congress. In practice, this is a renewal of an existing stance rather than a new policy, and it will remain in effect for one year unless ended earlier or extended again.
